title: Four People, One Score
scopeNote: This keeps the logistic model with its coefficients printed, the four colleagues who share an attitude score, and the demonstration that the attitude-behaviour correlation depends on how much the conditions vary. The correspondence control, the per-person factor sliders and the guided prediction round are in the longer version. The scale is fixed at the behaviour-level weight, which is the favourable case, so the gap cannot be dismissed as an artefact of asking the wrong question.
summary: Four fictional colleagues with identical attitude scores speak up in 25, 8, 4 and 14 of thirty meetings, and across three hundred people the attitude-behaviour correlation more than doubles when everybody is put in the same kind of room.
learningObjectives: Explain why a strong attitude does not on its own predict the behaviour.
Distinguish factors that shift the odds from opportunity, which multiplies.
Explain why an intervention aimed at an attitude can change nothing.
Explain why an average across people with different conditions is not a prediction about any of them.
Explain why a low attitude-behaviour correlation is partly a measurement of how unequal the conditions are.
interactionTypes: a prediction from a single attitude score
four colleagues with identical scores and different behaviour
a guided change of one factor for one person
a toggle between two workplaces holding all three hundred attitude scores constant
a scatter in which markers move vertically and never horizontally
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. No questionnaire is administered to the reader.
dataStatus: Four fictional colleagues and three hundred simulated ones. The coefficients are invented and printed on screen, the correlations that follow from them are not findings, and no number estimates anything.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout. Every factor for every colleague is in a real table with row and column headers, so the model's inputs are never hidden behind a figure, and each person's situation is also given in prose. The workplace control is a button carrying aria-pressed with a visible word saying which version is in use, and both correlations are readouts as well as being visible in the scatter. The chart description gives both correlations and states which one is currently shown. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
simulationNotes: The model is logistic in the reasoned-action family, with the coefficients printed on the page: attitude weighted by a correspondence of 0.70, plus norm, perceived control and habit, minus constraint, all passed through the logistic and then multiplied by opportunity. Opportunity multiplying rather than adding is the structural point, and the guided button demonstrates it by raising Marek's opportunity alone from 0.15 to 0.85, which takes him from 4 meetings out of 30 to 24 while every other number in his row stays put. The four colleagues share an attitude of 0.86 and produce 25, 8, 4 and 14, a spread of 21 meetings. Every figure quoted in the feedback is computed from the model rather than written in, so a change to a coefficient cannot leave the prose contradicting the table. One design correction is worth recording. Plotting the model's probability against attitude under uniform conditions gives a correlation of essentially one, because with the conditions fixed the probability is a deterministic function of the attitude; that is true of the model and reads as an artefact. What a study observes is a behaviour, so each of the three hundred is observed over thirty meetings and the plotted value is the share in which they spoke up. Binomial variation then behaves as it does in real data and the correlation comes out at 0.26 in varying conditions against 0.61 in uniform ones, both of which are in the range real studies report. The attitude scores and the per-person occasion draws are generated once and reused by both regimes, so nothing about any of the three hundred differs between the two pictures; the test suite checks this by comparing the rendered horizontal positions of all three hundred markers before and after the toggle. Simplifications, stated in the caution: six factors is a deliberate reduction, and the model has no feedback in it at all, which is its largest omission.
readmeTopic: why the same attitude produces completely different behaviour, and what that does to a correlation
